pages.title: Two ways to express gas composition

blocks.text: A gas mixture can be measured through concentrations or partial pressures. The two textbook equilibrium forms are related through the ideal-gas equation, provided the unit convention and approximation are explicit.
For each ideal gas, p(i) = [i]RT. Substitute this separately for every partial pressure in K(p), retaining the stoichiometric powers.

pages.transition: Collect the factors of RT from numerator and denominator.

pages.title: Derive the gas-coefficient exponent

blocks.text: For aA(g) + bB(g) ⇌ cC(g) + dD(g), substitution gives K(p) = K(c)(RT)^(c+d−a−b). Define Δn(g) as gaseous-product coefficients minus gaseous-reactant coefficients: K(p) = K(c)(RT)^Δn(g).
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ has Δn(g) = −2. H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI has Δn(g) = 0, so the corresponding numerical forms agree. Count only gas coefficients.

pages.transition: Choose an R value matching pressure and volume units.

pages.title: Worked K(p) conversion

blocks.text: Teacher-created data: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) has K(c) = 0.100 in the stated concentration convention at 300 K. Δn(g) = 1. Using R = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, K(p) = 0.100 × 0.08314 × 300 = 2.49 in the corresponding bar convention.
Numerical comparisons between K(p) and K(c) require stated units. A positive Δn(g) alone is not a unit-independent claim that one numerical constant must always be larger.

pages.transition: Different phases introduce another useful simplification.

pages.title: Pure solids and liquids are not variable terms

blocks.text: Heterogeneous equilibrium contains more than one phase. A pure solid or pure liquid has activity taken as one, so its contribution is incorporated into K rather than written as a variable concentration.
For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), the textbook forms are K(p) = p(CO₂) and K(c) = [CO₂]. Both solids must remain present for this coexistence condition.

pages.transition: An aqueous solute is different from a separate pure phase.

pages.title: Read phase labels before omitting a term

blocks.text: For Ni(s) + 4CO(g) ⇌ Ni(CO)₄(g), K(c) = [Ni(CO)₄]/[CO]⁴. Solid nickel is omitted, but the two gaseous substances remain.

Dissolved ions and molecules normally retain variable activities. Water as bulk solvent is commonly incorporated into dilute aqueous constants, but a solute labelled aqueous is not a separate pure liquid.
Aqueous means dissolved in water. It does not mean the dissolved substance itself is liquid water.

pages.transition: The magnitude of a correctly written K describes equilibrium preference.

pages.title: K describes extent, not speed

blocks.text: A very large K generally indicates product-favoured equilibrium for the written equation; a very small K indicates reactant-favoured equilibrium. NCERT uses rough guides above 10³ and below 10⁻³ for strongly favoured sides.
K does not reveal the rate of approaching equilibrium. A reaction with a large K can be slow. Nor does K alone determine each concentration without the starting amounts and stoichiometry.

pages.transition: A present mixture needs comparison with the equilibrium ratio.

pages.title: Q predicts which way a mixture changes

blocks.text: The reaction quotient Q has the same expression as K but uses current concentrations or pressures, whether or not the mixture is at equilibrium. At equilibrium Q = K.
Q < K favours net forward change; Q > K favours net reverse change; Q = K gives no net change. For A ⇌ B with K = 4, a current [B]/[A] = 1 favours more B, while a ratio of 10 favours more A.

pages.transition: Use stoichiometry to find an unknown equilibrium composition.

pages.title: Build an initial–change–equilibrium account

blocks.text: Write initial concentrations, then let x describe a reaction change. Use balanced coefficients to obtain each species’ change, and add it to the initial value before substituting into K.
For A ⇌ B starting with 1.00 M A and no B, equilibrium values are 1.00 − x and x. The possible range is 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.00 M. For A ⇌ 2B the B change would instead be +2x.

pages.transition: Solve the account and check whether its answer is physically possible.

pages.title: Worked equilibrium concentrations

blocks.text: Teacher-created example: A ⇌ B has K = 4.00 and initially 1.00 M A only. Required equilibrium composition. K = x/(1.00 − x) = 4.00. Hence x = 4.00 − 4.00x; 5.00x = 4.00; x = 0.800 M. Therefore [A] = 0.200 M and [B] = 0.800 M.
Verify: 0.800/0.200 = 4.00, and both concentrations are nonnegative. A mathematical root producing negative concentration must be rejected.
For quadratic accounts, compare candidate roots with the full physical range, not merely their signs. A positive x can still consume more reactant than was initially present.

pages.transition: Revise the gas conversion, phase rule and quotient calculation together.

pages.title: Revision: form the correct ratio first

blocks.text: Ideal-gas textbook forms satisfy K(p) = K(c)(RT)^Δn(g) with matching units. Pure solid and liquid activities are omitted; variable gas and solute activities remain.

K describes equilibrium preference, Q/K describes current direction, and an initial–change–equilibrium account supplies unknown concentrations. Check coefficients, physical roots and substitution back into the original expression.

questions.question: Does adding more CaCO₃(s) change K at fixed temperature?
questions.answer: No. K depends on temperature, and changing a pure solid amount does not enter the expression while that phase remains.

questions.question: What is Δn(g) for PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g)?
questions.answer: 2 − 1 = +1, giving K(p) = K(c)RT in the corresponding textbook conventions.

questions.question: If Q = 20 and K = 5, which way is net reaction?
questions.answer: Reverse, lowering the product-to-reactant ratio toward K.

questions.question: Does a large K imply a fast reaction?
questions.answer: No. It describes equilibrium composition, not the kinetic rate.

questions.question: For A ⇌ 2B, what concentration changes follow consumption of x M A?
questions.answer: A changes by −x and B by +2x.

questions.question: Why reject a negative equilibrium concentration root?
questions.answer: It is physically impossible even if it solves a rearranged algebraic equation.
